title: Phishing, social engineering and email security
summary: Why people are the most attacked surface: persuasion levers, phishing types, how SMTP mail moves, SPF, DKIM and DMARC, header triage, lookalike domains, AiTM, passkeys and BEC.
outcomes: Explain which persuasion levers a lure pulls and which process rules neutralise them
Trace an email through SMTP and MX records and tell envelope-from, header From and display name apart
Read SPF, DKIM and DMARC records and predict the DMARC verdict for a message
Triage a reported message from its raw headers, trusting only your own server's results
Recognise lookalike and homoglyph domains, malicious links and attachment tricks
Explain why AiTM phishing beats codes and push prompts but not passkeys
Describe how BEC and invoice fraud work and the controls and SOC workflow that stop them

lessons.title: Why people are the most attacked surface

blocks.md:
Picture a company with patched servers, a firewall and encrypted disks. An attacker who wants its money does not need a software bug. They send one email to the person who pays invoices: "Our bank details changed, please use the new account for this month." If that person believes it, the money leaves through the company's own, fully working payment process.

That is **social engineering**: getting a person to do something that helps the attacker (reveal a password, open a file, approve a login, send money) by manipulating what they believe, rather than by breaking a machine.

**Phishing** is social engineering delivered by a message: an email, text or call that pretends to come from someone trusted so that the target hands over something valuable. The name started as "fishing" for passwords on America Online (AOL) in the mid-1990s. Koceilah Rekouche, who wrote the AOL hacking tool AOHell, recalls in a 2011 paper that the group called the trick "fishing" and that they changed the spelling to "phishing" in AOHell, which began automating it in January 1995.

Why aim at people? A server bug gets patched once and is fixed for every user. A person's willingness to help a colleague, obey a boss or hurry before a deadline cannot be patched, and every employee with an inbox is a door.

blocks.title: One email, five steps to a loss

scenes.caption: The attacker only needs to reach an inbox. Email is open by design: anyone on the Internet can send a message to any address.
The person acts: clicks a link and types a password, opens an attachment, or simply replies. This is the step social engineering targets.
The action converts to access: a stolen password, malware running on the laptop, or a conversation the attacker controls.
Access converts to the goal: money wired, data stolen, or ransomware. Defences can break the chain at any arrow, not only at the person.
Where defenders cut the chain: filtering stops delivery, phishing-resistant logins make stolen passwords useless, payment checks stop the wire. Later lessons cover each.

blocks.md: How big is it? The FBI's **IC3** (Internet Crime Complaint Center, the FBI unit that collects cybercrime reports from victims) publishes yearly totals. In its 2025 report, "phishing/spoofing" was among the most reported crime types with 191,561 complaints, while **BEC** (business email compromise: tricking a business into paying the wrong party by email, covered in lesson 13) had 24,768 complaints but USD 3,046,598,558 in reported losses.

blocks.title: IC3 2025: many phishing reports, few but costly BEC losses

scenes.caption: Complaints in thousands. Phishing is reported about eight times as often as BEC, because almost everyone receives it.
Reported losses in millions of USD. BEC losses (about 3,047) dwarf the losses filed under phishing itself (about 216).
Loss per complaint in thousands of USD: about 1.1 for phishing and 123.0 for BEC, roughly 109 times more. Phishing is usually the door; the loss lands later.

blocks.md:
The numbers need care. IC3 counts only what victims report, and one incident can sit in several categories: a phish that steals a mailbox password and ends in a fake invoice is often filed as BEC. Read them as a lower bound and as a picture of where money goes, not as a precise census.

Throughout this course you will read real messages as data. Below is the raw text of a tiny email, as defined by **RFC 5322** (an RFC, Request for Comments, is a numbered document in the Internet's official technical series, which includes its standards; many are published by the IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force; 5322 is the one that defines the email message format). Lines before the blank line are **header fields**; the rest is the **body**.

blocks.code:
From: "Accounts Payable" <ap@supplier.example>
To: pat@corp.example
Subject: Updated bank details for invoice 4471
Date: Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:02:11 +0000
Message-ID: <77f1@supplier.example>

Hi Pat, our bank changed. Please pay invoice 4471
to the new account in the attached letter today.
blocks.caption: Five header fields, a blank line, then the body. Nothing in this format proves who wrote it: every header is plain text the sender typed.

blocks.md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

Common misconception: "only careless people fall for phishing". The UK NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) notes that people click for many reasons, including situational ones such as being busy and stressed, and that blaming them does not work. Blame also stops people reporting mistakes, which is the signal defenders need most.

blocks.question: A company patches every server within a day of each release. Why does that not reduce its phishing risk much?
options: Phishing only works against unpatched browsers
Patching makes email filters less accurate
Phishing manipulates a person into using legitimate access, so no software flaw needs to exist
Phishing only targets home users, not companies
blocks.explain: A phish succeeds when a person types a password, approves a prompt or sends money through a normal process. Every step uses working software as designed, so patch speed barely matters. Malicious attachments can add a software exploit, but many phish need none.

blocks.question: IC3 2025 shows about 191,561 phishing complaints and 24,768 BEC complaints, but BEC losses are about 14 times larger. What best explains this?
options: Phishing is often the entry step, while BEC is where large wire transfers are lost
BEC victims exaggerate their losses
Phishing has stopped causing any losses
BEC complaints are counted in a different currency
blocks.explain: Phishing is the common first step: it steals passwords or opens conversations. BEC is the monetising step, where a single fraudulent wire can be millions. The categories overlap, so the totals are a rough picture, not exact accounting.

lessons.title: The persuasion levers every lure pulls

blocks.md:
Try this message: "This is Dana (CEO). I need gift cards for a client before my 3 pm meeting, keep it quiet, I will pay you back." It uses no technology at all. It works, when it works, because it presses on shortcuts every person uses to decide quickly.

Robert Cialdini, a social psychologist who has studied compliance for decades, groups these shortcuts into principles of persuasion. Cialdini's site lists seven: **reciprocity** (we repay what we were given), **scarcity** (we want what is running out), **authority** (we follow credible experts and bosses), **consistency** (we act in line with what we already said or did), **liking** (we say yes to people we like or who resemble us), **social proof** (we copy what others like us do) and **unity** (we favour people we see as part of our group).

Frank Stajano, a security researcher at the University of Cambridge, and Paul Wilson, a performer on the BBC programme *The Real Hustle* who recreated street scams on camera, studied those scams in a 2009 Cambridge technical report and drew seven principles from the victims' side. Three map straight onto phishing:

- **Social compliance**: "society trains people not to question authority", so a fake police officer, IT technician or CEO is obeyed.
- **Time**: under time pressure people switch to a decision strategy with less reasoning. Phishing's "urgency" is this principle.
- **Distraction**: while attention is on the prize or the threat, the details that would expose the trick go unchecked.

Their point for engineers: these are not individual failings but stable behaviour, so systems must be designed around them.

blocks.title: Which levers do common lures pull?

scenes.caption: Rows are real lure styles, columns are levers. A 1 means the lure leans on that lever. Most lures combine two or three.
Authority: the CEO wire request and the fake IT help desk call both borrow a boss or expert's standing. In the Twitter 2020 case (next lesson), callers claimed to be internal IT.
Urgency (Stajano and Wilson's time principle): deadlines like 'expires in 2 hours' push people into fast, shallow decisions.
Scarcity and reciprocity: 'only 3 seats left' and 'here is a free gift card, just fill the survey' create a feeling of loss or debt.
Social proof: 'your colleagues have already signed' makes compliance feel normal. The shared-document lure uses it with liking.

blocks.code:
From: "IT Service Desk" <servicedesk@corp-it.example>   # authority: IT
Subject: [Action required] Password expires in 2 hours   # urgency

Hi Pat,                                                  # liking: uses your name
Your password expires at 11:00 today. 1,204 colleagues   # social proof
have already moved to the new sign-in page.
Re-validate now to keep access to payroll:               # loss of something you value
  https://corp-it.example/sso/renew
Thanks for helping us keep Corp secure!
blocks.caption: A typical credential lure, annotated (the # comments are ours). Every line presses a lever; none of it needs a technical exploit.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.** You cannot remove these shortcuts from people, so remove their power over the process:

- **Pre-commit to rules that ignore the lever.** "Bank detail changes are always confirmed by phone on the number in our vendor file, even if the CEO asks." Authority and urgency then have nothing to push on.
- **Make the safe path the fast path.** A one-click report button costs less effort than investigating.
- **Say it out loud.** If leadership says "I will never ask you to buy gift cards or skip a payment check", an email that does so contradicts authority instead of borrowing it.

Detection signals that map to levers: urgency words in subject lines, a display name with a title ("CEO") on an external address, and requests for secrecy.

Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

blocks.prompt: A finance clerk gets a call from someone claiming to be the CFO, who is travelling and needs an urgent payment approved within 30 minutes. Which two levers are being pulled, and what single process rule defeats both?
blocks.reveal: Authority (the CFO) and urgency (30 minutes). A rule such as "every new payment or bank change is verified by calling back a number from our own records, and no deadline overrides this" defeats both: the clerk does not have to judge whether the caller is real, only follow the rule. The FBI's BEC guidance gives the same advice: use secondary channels to verify requests for changes in account information.

blocks.question: Which pair best matches Stajano and Wilson's 'time' principle and Cialdini's 'authority' principle in a phishing email?
options: 'Your mailbox is 98 percent full' and 'Click to view your photo'
'Thanks for your order' and 'Your colleagues liked this post'
'Unsubscribe here' and 'Sent from my iPhone'
'Reply within 1 hour or your account is closed' and 'Message from the Head of Security'
blocks.explain: The deadline is time pressure, which pushes fast and shallow decisions. A sender styled as a head of security borrows authority. The other pairs mix weaker cues (curiosity, reciprocity, social proof) or none.

blocks.question: Why does a written rule like 'all bank detail changes are confirmed by phone on a number we already hold' work better than training people to judge each request?
options: It makes emails load faster
It removes the need for the person to resist authority or urgency in the moment, because the rule decides
It stops attackers from sending email
It guarantees that the CEO never travels
blocks.explain: Levers work on in-the-moment judgement. A pre-committed rule takes the decision out of that moment, and using a number you already hold means the attacker cannot supply the callback number themselves.

lessons.title: From mass phishing to help-desk calls

blocks.md:
Phishing varies along two dials: **how targeted** the message is, and **which channel** carries it.

On the targeting dial:
- **Mass phishing**: one generic lure ("Your parcel is held, pay the fee") sent to huge lists. It needs only a tiny success rate.
- **Spear phishing**: a lure built for one person or a small group, using research (role, colleagues, current projects). The UK NCSC uses this name for targeted campaigns that use information about employees or the company to be more persuasive.
- **Whaling**: spear phishing aimed at a "big phish", in the NCSC's words, such as a board member with access to valuable assets.

On the channel dial:
- **Smishing**: SMS phishing. SMS is Short Message Service, the text-message system of mobile networks; smishing = SMS + phishing.
- **Vishing**: voice phishing, by phone call; vishing = voice + phishing.
- **QR-code phishing** (sometimes "quishing"): a QR code (Quick Response code, a square barcode a phone camera reads) that leads to a malicious site. The FBI [warned in 2022](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2022/PSA220118) that criminals tamper with both digital and physical QR codes, for example a sticker placed on top of a real code.
- **Help-desk social engineering**: the attacker calls the company's IT help desk pretending to be an employee, and asks for a password reset or a new MFA device. **MFA** (multi-factor authentication) means a login needs a second factor such as a phone prompt or code, in addition to the password.

Channels outside email matter because email has filters and authentication checks (lessons 6 to 8). A phone call has neither.

**Case: Twitter, July 2020.** The New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS, the state's financial regulator) investigated how a 17-year-old and accomplices took over celebrity accounts. On 14 July the attackers phoned several Twitter employees, claiming to be from the IT help desk about a VPN problem (a VPN, virtual private network, is the encrypted tunnel remote staff use to reach the internal network). VPN problems were common after the move to remote work, which made the story believable. Employees were directed to a phishing site that looked identical to Twitter's VPN login, on a similarly named domain.

blocks.title: Twitter 2020: a phone call plus a relayed login

scenes.caption: The call: an 'IT help desk' voice about a real, familiar problem. Authority plus a plausible pretext.
The employee is sent to a lookalike VPN login page that the attackers control.
The employee types their username and password into the fake page.
In real time, the attackers type the same credentials into Twitter's real login.
The real site sends the MFA prompt to the employee's phone. The employee, expecting a login, approves it.
The session belongs to the attackers. They used it to learn the intranet, then targeted staff with access to account tools.

blocks.md:
Per the NYDFS report, the first compromised employee lacked access to the account tools, so the attackers studied the intranet and on 15 July targeted staff who had it. In all, 130 accounts were compromised, 45 were used to tweet a "double your bitcoin" scam, and the attackers took about USD 118,000 in bitcoin. Some employees did report the calls; at least one believed them.

The report's main technical lesson: Twitter used app-based MFA, which the attackers beat by getting employees to approve the prompt. It said a hardware security key "would have stopped the Hackers", and Twitter moved to them. Lesson 12 explains why.

**Case: MGM Resorts, September 2023.** MGM, a casino and hotel operator on the Las Vegas Strip, shut down large parts of its network after a breach; slot machines and thousands of hotel key cards stopped working. Researchers attributed it to the group called **Scattered Spider**, which, the Financial Times [reported](https://arstechnica.com/security/2023/09/a-phone-call-to-helpdesk-was-likely-all-it-took-to-hack-mgm/), uses fraudulent phone calls to employees and help desks, and a call to the help desk was reported as the likely way in.

The US cybersecurity agency **CISA** (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and the FBI describe the pattern in advisory AA23-320A: calls first learn how password resets work, then gather details about a target employee, then convince help-desk staff to reset passwords or move MFA to an attacker's device.

blocks.code:
# Help-desk reset policy (illustrative)
reset_password_or_mfa:
  require:
    - caller_authenticates_with: existing_passkey   # proves they hold the old factor
    - or:
        - video_call_with_photo_id: true
        - manager_approval_via: ticket_system       # second person, separate channel
  never_accept:
    - employee_id_or_date_of_birth_alone            # easy to find or buy
    - callback_number_given_by_caller
  after_reset:
    - notify_user_on: [old_phone, manager]
    - alert_soc_if: new_mfa_device_and_new_location
blocks.caption: A help desk policy as YAML (a plain-text configuration format). Mandiant's (Google's incident response firm) hardening guidance for this group recommends positive identity checks such as on-camera or in-person verification, and strong authentication before changing MFA methods.

blocks.md: **Defender view for voice and help-desk attacks.** Prevention: phishing-resistant MFA (security keys or passkeys) so a relayed password and approved prompt are not enough; reset procedures that need a factor the attacker lacks, as in [Mandiant's hardening guidance](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc3944-proactive-hardening-recommendations/) for this group. Detection: identity logs showing a password reset or new MFA device followed by a login from an unfamiliar location or device; calls that employees report. Response: revoke the account's sessions, undo the MFA change, and check what the session touched.

blocks.question: An attacker texts 300 employees 'Your parcel could not be delivered, pay 1.99 to rebook' with a link. Which term fits best?
options: Whaling
Mass smishing
Spear phishing by voice
Help-desk social engineering
blocks.explain: It is generic (mass) and arrives by SMS (smishing). Whaling targets a senior individual; spear phishing is tailored; help-desk attacks target IT staff by phone.

blocks.question: Twitter staff had MFA in July 2020. Why did it not stop the attack?
options: MFA was switched off during remote work
The attackers guessed the six-digit codes
The attackers relayed the password to the real site at once, and employees approved the resulting MFA prompt
MFA only protects email, not VPNs
blocks.explain: The MFA prompt was real; the person approving it believed they were logging in. App-based approval cannot tell which site the person is actually looking at. A security key checks the site's domain itself, so it would not have signed in for the lookalike page.

lessons.title: How an email actually moves: SMTP and MX records

blocks.md:
To judge whether an email is forged you must know how a real one travels. Say Ana at `supplier.example` writes to Pat at `corp.example`. Four kinds of program touch the message:

- An **MUA** (mail user agent: the app a person reads and writes mail in, such as Outlook or a webmail page) where Ana writes it.
- Ana's provider's **MTA** (mail transfer agent: a server that relays mail toward its destination), which accepts it from Ana's app.
- Pat's provider's MTA, the server listed for `corp.example` in DNS, which receives it.
- Pat's MUA, which shows it from the mailbox.

Servers talk to each other with **SMTP** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), first defined in RFC 821 in 1982; today's version is RFC 5321. Servers listen for it on TCP port 25.

How does Ana's server know where `corp.example` receives mail? It asks DNS (you met DNS in the networking course: the Internet's name lookup system) for the domain's **MX records** (mail exchanger records: the hosts that accept mail for a domain). Each MX has a preference number; RFC 5321 says lower numbers are more preferred, and a sender tries them in that order. Here is a real lookup for gmail.com:

blocks.code:
dig +short MX gmail.com
5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
10 alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
20 alt2.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
30 alt3.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
40 alt4.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
blocks.caption: Queried November 2026 (sorted by preference). A sender tries the preference-5 host first and falls back to the others if it is unreachable.

blocks.title: The path of one message

scenes.caption: Ana writes the message in a mail app (MUA) and submits it to the provider's server, after logging in to it.
Ana's server asks DNS: who receives mail for corp.example? The MX answer names mx.corp.example.
Ana's server opens a TCP connection to mx.corp.example on port 25 and hands over the message with SMTP. No password is involved: any server may deliver to an MX.
Each receiving server adds a Received header at the top recording who connected and from which IP. Then the message is stored in Pat's mailbox.
Pat's app fetches the message from the mailbox. Pat sees only what the headers claim, unless the receiving server checked them (lessons 6 to 8).

blocks.md: The SMTP conversation itself is plain text: the client sends commands, the server answers with three-digit reply codes (2xx means success, 3xx means "go on", 4xx and 5xx are temporary and permanent errors). The commands that matter for security are `MAIL FROM`, which names the **envelope sender** (where bounces go), and `RCPT TO`, which names each recipient. After `DATA` comes the message itself, headers and body, ended by a line with a single dot.

blocks.title: One SMTP session, command by command

scenes.caption: The server greets with code 220. The client introduces itself with EHLO (extended hello) and a hostname of its choice.
MAIL FROM sets the envelope sender. The server records it but, in plain SMTP, does not verify it.
RCPT TO names a recipient. The server checks only that it accepts mail for that address.
DATA, a 354 'go ahead', then the full message (From:, To:, Subject:, body) ending with a lone dot.
The server takes responsibility for delivery (250) and the client says goodbye (221). Nothing in this exchange proved who Ana is.

blocks.md: On arrival, RFC 5321 requires every SMTP server to **prepend** a `Received` header (add it at the top) and never change or remove earlier ones. Its `from` clause should contain both the name the client gave in EHLO and the IP address seen on the actual TCP connection. The name is a claim; the IP is what the receiving server observed. The final server also adds `Return-Path` to record the envelope sender. So a delivered message's headers read like a stack, newest on top:

blocks.code:
Return-Path: <ana@supplier.example>
Received: from smtp.supplier.example (smtp.supplier.example [192.0.2.25])
        by mx.corp.example with ESMTPS id 7F3A; Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:02:13 +0000
Received: from [10.1.4.20] (unknown [198.51.100.40])
        by smtp.supplier.example with ESMTPSA id c9e1; Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:02:12 +0000
From: "Ana Lima" <ana@supplier.example>
To: pat@corp.example
Subject: Invoice 4471
blocks.caption: Read Received headers bottom to top to follow the path: Ana's laptop submitted to smtp.supplier.example, which relayed to mx.corp.example. Only the top one was written by Pat's own server. ESMTPS: SMTP with extensions over TLS; ESMTPSA: the same, client logged in (RFC 3848).

blocks.md: Only Received headers added by servers you control are trustworthy. Anything below your own border server's Received line was written before the message reached you, possibly by the attacker.

blocks.question: A message has three Received headers. Which one was written by your own receiving server, and what in it can you trust most?
options: The top one; the IP address your server saw on the TCP connection
The bottom one; the EHLO name
The middle one; the date
Any of them; all Received headers are verified by DNS
blocks.explain: Servers prepend, so your server's header is on top. Its IP address came from the actual connection, while the EHLO name is whatever the client chose to say. Lower headers could have been written by anyone, including the sender.

blocks.question: In the SMTP session, which command sets the address that bounces are sent to?
options: RCPT TO
EHLO
MAIL FROM
The From: header inside DATA
blocks.explain: MAIL FROM sets the envelope sender, also called the reverse-path; bounce messages go there, and the final server records it as Return-Path. The From: header inside DATA is what people see, and it can differ, which is the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.title: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works

blocks.md:
A paper letter has two senders: the return address on the **envelope**, which the post office uses if delivery fails, and the letterhead **inside**, which the reader sees. The post office never checks that they match. Email copies this design, and the SMTP standard itself calls the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO part the "envelope".

So every email carries at least three "from" identities:

1. **Envelope-from** (written RFC5321.MailFrom after the SMTP standard): the address in `MAIL FROM`. Used for bounces; recorded as `Return-Path`. Most people never see it.
2. **Header-from** (RFC5322.From after the message-format standard): the `From:` header inside the message. This is the address mail apps display.
3. **Display name**: the free-text label before the address in the From header, as in `"Dana Ruiz" <dana@corp.example>`. Many apps, especially on phones, show only this.

Plus `Reply-To:`, which tells the app where replies should go, and may point anywhere.

Plain SMTP verifies none of these. The receiving server accepts whatever text the client sends after `MAIL FROM`, and the From header is just a line inside the DATA. **Spoofing** is putting someone else's identity in these fields. The rest of this course is largely about adding checks that SMTP lacks.

There are legitimate reasons for the identities to differ, which is why servers cannot simply demand they match. A newsletter sent through a mailing service often has an envelope-from at the service (so the service gets the bounces) and a header-from at the brand.

blocks.title: Three identities, three audiences

scenes.caption: The SMTP envelope: MAIL FROM is read by servers and used for bounces. In this newsletter it belongs to the mailing service.
The header From is inside the message. Mail apps show it, so this is the identity a person trusts.
The display name is free text. A phone app may show only 'Dana Ruiz' and hide the address entirely.
Reply-To decides where an answer goes. In fraud it often points to the attacker's mailbox while From looks right.
Plain SMTP checks none of the four. SPF (lesson 6) checks the envelope, DKIM (lesson 7) signs headers, DMARC (lesson 8) ties them to the header From.

blocks.code:
EHLO mail.cheap-host.example
MAIL FROM:<x7@cheap-host.example>      [envelope: attacker's own domain]
RCPT TO:<ap-team@corp.example>
DATA
From: "Dana Ruiz, CEO" <dana.ruiz@corp.example>   [header: forged]
Reply-To: dana.ruiz.ceo@freemail.example          [replies go to attacker]
Subject: Urgent wire before 11:00

Can you process a payment today? I am in meetings, email only.
.
blocks.caption: A spoofed CEO message as raw SMTP (the bracketed notes are ours). Without SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks, the receiving server would accept and display it as from dana.ruiz@corp.example.

blocks.md:
Attackers use four main forms, and each needs a different defence:

- **Exact-domain spoofing**: header From uses the real domain (`dana.ruiz@corp.example`). DMARC with an enforcing policy stops this, as lesson 8 shows.
- **Display-name spoofing**: a real free-mail account with display name "Dana Ruiz, CEO". It passes every authentication check, because the attacker really owns that address. Only showing the address, or an "external sender" banner, helps.
- **Lookalike domains**: `corp-example.com` or a domain with look-alike Unicode letters (lesson 10). Also passes authentication, for the attacker's own domain.
- **Compromised real accounts**: the attacker logged into a genuine mailbox. Every check passes; only behaviour gives it away (lesson 13).

**Case: John Podesta, March 2016.** The 2018 US indictment of twelve officers of the GRU (Russia's military intelligence agency) describes how, on or about 19 March 2016, they sent a spearphishing email to the chairman of Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign (the indictment does not give the name; the chairman was John Podesta). They altered the appearance of the sender address so the email looked like a **security notification from Google** (the indictment's own example of "spoofing"), told the recipient to change the password via an embedded link, and hid the real destination behind a URL-shortening service. The instructions were followed, and on about 21 March the conspirators stole the account's contents: over 50,000 emails.

Note the levers: authority (Google security) and fear of loss (someone has your account), plus a link whose real target was hidden.

Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

Defender view: external-sender banners ("This message came from outside the organisation") mark display-name spoofs of internal staff. Many gateways also flag inbound mail whose display name matches an executive's name but whose address is external. Detection signal in mail logs: header From domain or display name differs from envelope-from or Reply-To domain.

blocks.question: An email shows 'From: PayPal Security' on a phone. The underlying address is security@paypal-help.example and DMARC for paypal-help.example passes. What kind of spoof is this?
options: A display-name spoof combined with a lookalike domain the attacker owns
Exact-domain spoofing that DMARC failed to stop
A legitimate message, because DMARC passed
Envelope-from forgery only
blocks.explain: The attacker owns paypal-help.example, so authentication for that domain passes. The display name carries the deception. DMARC protects paypal.com's exact domain, not names that merely resemble it.

blocks.question: Why can receiving servers not simply reject every message whose envelope-from differs from its header From?
options: Because SMTP forbids comparing them
Because the header From is encrypted
Because envelope-from is always empty
Because mailing services legitimately use their own bounce address while sending as a brand's From address
blocks.explain: Bulk senders, ticketing systems and forwarders routinely use a different envelope-from to collect bounces. DMARC solves this with alignment rules that allow related domains instead of demanding an exact match everywhere.

lessons.title: SPF: which servers may send for a domain

blocks.md:
The simplest fix for a forged envelope: let each domain publish the list of servers allowed to send its mail, and let receivers check the connecting IP against that list. That is **SPF** (Sender Policy Framework, RFC 7208): the sending domain publishes a policy listing the hosts allowed to send its mail, and receivers check it.

The list lives in DNS as a TXT record (a DNS record type that holds free text) at the domain itself. Tiny example: `corp.example` sends from its own network 192.0.2.0/24 and through a mailing service.

blocks.code:
corp.example.          TXT "v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 include:_spf.mailer.example -all"
_spf.mailer.example.   TXT "v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.0/24 -all"

; real records, queried November 2026
google.com.            TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
_spf.google.com.       TXT "v=spf1 ip4:74.125.0.0/16 ip4:209.85.128.0/17 ip6:2001:4860:4864::/56 ... ~all"
blocks.caption: Zone-file style (lines after ; are comments). The real _spf.google.com record lists more ranges than shown here.

blocks.md:
Read a record left to right. `v=spf1` marks it as SPF. Then come **mechanisms**, each a test that matches or not:

- `ip4:` / `ip6:` match if the client IP is in the range.
- `include:` runs the whole check against another domain's record and matches if that returns pass. It is how you authorise a provider.
- `a` and `mx` match the domain's own address or MX hosts.
- `all` always matches, so it goes last as the default.

Each mechanism may carry a **qualifier** that sets the result if it matches: `+` pass (the default), `-` fail, `~` softfail (a weak statement that the host is probably not authorised), `?` neutral (no assertion). If nothing matches, the result is neutral; if there is no SPF record, none.

blocks.title: Evaluating SPF for three client IPs

scenes.caption: The receiver has the client IP from the TCP connection and the domain from MAIL FROM. It fetches corp.example's record and walks its terms.
First term ip4:192.0.2.0/24. 203.0.113.9 is not in that range, so no match; move on.
include: costs one DNS lookup (the limit is 10) and evaluates _spf.mailer.example with the same IP.
Inside the include, 203.0.113.9 is not in 198.51.100.0/24 and -all returns fail. A fail inside an include just means 'no match' outside.
The last term -all matches everything with qualifier '-', so the result is fail: this IP may not send as corp.example.
Running all three IPs: the company's own server passes, the mailing service passes through the include, the stranger fails.

blocks.md:
The code is simplified (real SPF also handles `a`, `mx`, `redirect`, macros and errors), but the logic matches RFC 7208's `check_host()`. Two rules from the RFC matter in practice:

- **The 10-lookup limit.** Terms that cause DNS queries (`include`, `a`, `mx`, `ptr`, `exists`, `redirect`) may total at most 10; exceeding it gives **permerror** (permanent error). That is not a pass, so mail from any server the check only reaches after the tenth lookup gets no SPF credit (evaluation runs left to right, so servers matched earlier still pass). Companies that keep adding `include:` lines for every service break their own SPF this way.
- **Errors are distinct results.** Temperror (temporary DNS failure) and permerror (broken record) are not the same as fail.

blocks.prompt: An attacker registers cheap-host.example, publishes 'v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.9 -all', and sends mail from 203.0.113.9 with MAIL FROM x7@cheap-host.example and header From: dana.ruiz@corp.example. What is the SPF result, and does it protect corp.example?
blocks.reveal: SPF **passes**: the check runs on the envelope domain cheap-host.example, which the attacker owns and authorised. SPF never looks at the header From, so the forged `dana.ruiz@corp.example` that the reader sees is untouched. This is the gap DMARC closes in lesson 8 by requiring the SPF-checked domain to align with the header From domain.

blocks.md:
SPF has a second weakness: **forwarding**. If Pat forwards mail from `corp.example` to a personal account, the forwarding server connects with its own IP, which is not in corp.example's record, so SPF fails at the final destination although nothing malicious happened. RFC 7208 discusses this. It is why SPF alone cannot be the basis for rejecting mail, and why DKIM, which survives forwarding, was needed.

**Defender view.** Publish an SPF record for every domain, including ones that never send mail (`v=spf1 -all` says "nobody sends as me"). Keep within 10 lookups. Receivers record the outcome in the `Authentication-Results` header as `spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=...`, which is what analysts read in lesson 9.
Misconception: "SPF pass means the sender is who they claim". SPF pass means only that the connecting IP is allowed to send for the **envelope** domain. That domain may be the attacker's own.

blocks.question: corp.example's record is 'v=spf1 include:a.example include:b.example ... -all' with 11 include terms, each listing only ip4 ranges. Mail arrives from a server listed only in the 11th include. What happens?
options: SPF passes for everyone
Evaluation exceeds the DNS lookup limit and returns permerror
Only the first 10 includes are used
Receivers merge the extra include into the next record
blocks.explain: RFC 7208 caps DNS-querying terms at 10 during one evaluation. Reaching the 11th include exceeds the cap, so the result must be permerror, which is not a pass: this legitimate server gets no SPF credit. Servers matched earlier still pass.

blocks.question: Which is the strongest reason SPF alone is not enough to stop a forged CEO email?
options: SPF uses too much bandwidth
SPF checks the envelope domain, not the header From the reader sees
SPF only works over IPv6
SPF requires the recipient to install a plug-in
blocks.explain: The deception lives in the header From. SPF authenticates only the MAIL FROM (and HELO) domain, which the attacker can set to a domain they control.

lessons.title: DKIM: a signature over headers and body

blocks.md:
SPF ties mail to a server's IP, which breaks when mail is forwarded. A sturdier idea: let the sending domain **sign** the message itself, so the proof travels inside the message whatever path it takes.

That is **DKIM** (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376). It grew from DomainKeys, a design Mark Delany of Yahoo published as RFC 4870; the first DKIM standard (RFC 4871, 2007) had authors from Yahoo, Cisco, Sendmail and PGP Corporation. The name says what it does: a domain uses keys published in DNS to identify itself as taking responsibility for a message. As RFC 6376 puts it, a person, role or organisation that owns the signing domain can "claim some responsibility for a message".

The mechanism uses a **digital signature** (covered in depth in the crypto building blocks course; in one line: a value made with a private key that anyone with the matching public key can check, and that no one without the private key can forge):

1. The sending server computes a **hash** (a short fixed-size fingerprint; any change to the input changes it completely) of the body, called `bh=`.
2. It hashes a chosen list of headers, named in `h=` (From must always be included), plus the DKIM-Signature header itself with `bh=` filled in.
3. It signs that with the domain's private key and puts the result in `b=`.
4. The receiver fetches the public key from DNS at `<selector>._domainkey.<domain>`, where the domain is `d=` and the **selector** `s=` names which key (so a domain can have several and rotate them).

blocks.caption: a = algorithm, c = canonicalization for headers/body, d = signing domain, s = selector, h = signed headers, bh = body hash, b = signature. Keys and signature are shortened.

blocks.title: Signing on the way out, verifying on the way in

scenes.caption: The sending server hashes the body and the listed headers, signs with corp.example's private key, and adds the DKIM-Signature header.
The message travels, perhaps through a forwarder. Unlike SPF, nothing about the path matters.
The receiver reads d=corp.example and s=sel2026 and asks DNS for the public key.
It recomputes the body hash and checks the signature over the headers. Both match: dkim=pass with header.d=corp.example.

blocks.md: Why does tampering fail? Run the body-hash step yourself. **Canonicalization** (converting text to one standard form before hashing, so harmless changes do not break the signature) is "simple" here: trailing empty lines are reduced to one line ending. "relaxed" also tolerates changes in whitespace and header-name case.

blocks.code:
import base64
import hashlib

body = "Invoice attached.\r\n\r\n\r\n"

# "simple" body canonicalization (RFC 6376, 3.4.3):
# drop all empty lines at the end, keep one final CRLF
canon = body.rstrip("\r\n") + "\r\n"
digest = hashlib.sha256(canon.encode()).digest()
print("bh=" + base64.b64encode(digest).decode())

# change one character and hash again
tampered = canon.replace("Invoice", "invoice")
digest2 = hashlib.sha256(tampered.encode()).digest()
print("bh=" + base64.b64encode(digest2).decode())

# Output:
# bh=VNyDarC8YkEJy+BngMFk6o6Pz+FZqizy22SDHwG92S4=
# bh=dfWa9VT/KvXVdMOPhbdgzIDlrChI2L4rmfrhpGKpfIE=
blocks.caption: Python standard library only. For this body, relaxed body canonicalization gives the same bytes, so this is also the bh= in the c=relaxed/relaxed header above. Changing one capital letter produces an unrelated hash, so the stored bh= no longer matches and verification fails.

blocks.title: One changed letter, a completely different body hash

scenes.caption: The first 24 characters of the body hash for 'Invoice attached.' as the signer computed it.
Hash of 'invoice attached.': not one chunk matches. A verifier compares this with bh= in the signature and returns dkim=fail (body hash did not verify).

blocks.md:
What DKIM proves and what it does not:

- **Proves**: the domain in `d=` signed these headers and this body, and they were not changed in transit.
- **Does not prove**: that `d=` has anything to do with the From address. An attacker can sign with `d=attacker.example` and get dkim=pass. DMARC (next lesson) adds that link.
- **Breaks** when an intermediary edits the signed parts, for example a mailing list that adds "[list]" to the Subject or a footer to the body.

RFC 6376 also warns about the optional `l=` tag (sign only the first N bytes of the body): it lets someone append content after the signed part, which "might allow display of fraudulent content". RFC 6376 tells signers to be "extremely wary" of using it.

Defender view: sign all outbound mail with a key for your own domain (also when a provider sends for you), rotate keys by publishing a new selector, and remove old selectors' keys. In incident triage, `dkim=pass header.d=` tells you which domain vouched for a message; a pass for a domain you have never heard of is not reassurance.

blocks.question: A forwarded message arrives with SPF fail but DKIM pass for d=corp.example, and the From is corp.example. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The message was forged
DKIM always passes after forwarding
The forwarder's IP is not in corp.example's SPF record, but the signature survived because the content was unchanged
SPF and DKIM check the same thing, so one of them is broken
blocks.explain: Forwarding changes the connecting IP, which breaks SPF, but leaves the signed headers and body intact, so DKIM still verifies. This is exactly why DKIM was needed alongside SPF.

blocks.question: An attacker sends 'From: ceo@corp.example' signed with d=attacker.example using a valid key. What does the receiver's DKIM check report?
options: dkim=pass for attacker.example, which says nothing about corp.example
dkim=fail, because the domains differ
dkim=none, because the From is not signed
dkim=pass for corp.example
blocks.explain: DKIM verifies the signature for the d= domain only. Linking that domain to the From address is DMARC's job, through alignment.

blocks.question: A mailing list adds '[team]' to every Subject. The original signature listed Subject in h=. What happens to the original DKIM signature?
options: Nothing, Subject is never signed
It still verifies because relaxed canonicalization ignores added words
It fails, because a signed header changed
It is automatically re-signed by the original domain
blocks.explain: Relaxed canonicalization tolerates whitespace and header-name case, not new words. A changed signed header means the signature no longer verifies.

blocks.md:
SPF authenticates the envelope domain. DKIM authenticates the signing domain. Neither looks at the header From, the one address people read. **DMARC** (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) closes that gap. It was first published as RFC 7489 in 2015; the IETF standard that replaced it is RFC 9989 (May 2026), with reports defined in RFC 9990 and RFC 9991.

DMARC's core rule fits in one line: a message **passes DMARC** if SPF or DKIM passes **and** the domain that passed is **aligned** with the header From domain (DMARC calls it the Author Domain).

**Alignment** has two modes, chosen by the domain owner:

- **Relaxed** (the default): the two domains share the same **Organizational Domain**, roughly the registered domain such as `corp.example`, so `mail.corp.example` aligns with `news.corp.example`. RFC 9989 finds the Organizational Domain with a DNS "tree walk" up the name; earlier DMARC used a public list of domain suffixes.
- **Strict**: the two domains must be identical.

RFC 9989 explains why alignment is required: any domain owner, "even a bad actor", can publish SPF for its own domain and get an SPF pass, and a message "can bear a valid signature from any domain". Only a pass tied to the From domain says the domain's use was authorised.

blocks.caption: A simplified DMARC verdict in Python. Each case: header From domain | SPF result and domain | DKIM result and domain.

blocks.title: Five messages through the DMARC rule

scenes.caption: Rows are the five cases from the script; 1 means yes. DMARC needs one row where a pass and its alignment are both 1.
Newsletter via a mailing service: SPF passes for bounce.mailer.example, which does not align. DKIM passes for corp.example, which does. One aligned pass is enough.
Attacker: SPF and DKIM both pass, for attacker.example. Neither aligns with corp.example, so DMARC fails. This is the case SPF and DKIM alone missed.
Plain forgery from a stranger's server: SPF fails for corp.example and there is no signature. DMARC fails.
Subdomain: news.corp.example with SPF passing for mail.corp.example. Same Organizational Domain, so relaxed alignment passes even though DKIM failed.

blocks.md:
The domain owner publishes its **policy** as a TXT record at `_dmarc.<domain>`. The main tags (RFC 9989):

- `v=DMARC1` (required, first). `p=` the policy for mail that fails: `none` (no preference; just monitor), `quarantine` (treat as suspicious, usually the spam folder) or `reject` (refuse it during SMTP).
- `sp=` policy for existing subdomains, `np=` for subdomains that do not exist in DNS (an attacker's favourite: `payroll.corp.example`).
- `adkim=` / `aspf=` alignment mode, `r` (relaxed, default) or `s` (strict).
- `rua=` where to send **aggregate reports**, `ruf=` where to send **failure reports**, with `fo=` choosing when failure reports are made.
- `t=y` test mode: apply one level softer than stated. It replaces the old `pct=` tag, which RFC 9989 removed because receivers applied percentages inconsistently.

blocks.code:
_dmarc.corp.example.  TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@corp.example"

; real records, queried November 2026
_dmarc.google.com.  TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com"
_dmarc.gmail.com.   TXT "v=DMARC1; p=none; sp=quarantine; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com"
_dmarc.gov.uk.      TXT "v=DMARC1;p=reject;sp=none;np=reject;adkim=s;aspf=s;fo=1;rua=mailto:dmarc-rua@dmarc.service.gov.uk"
blocks.caption: gov.uk rejects failing mail, uses strict alignment and rejects mail from non-existent subdomains. Real records change; query them yourself with dig.

blocks.title: What a receiver does with a DMARC fail

scenes.caption: The receiver checks SPF and DKIM, then alignment with the header From. A pass simply joins normal filtering; DMARC pass is not a statement that the mail is safe.
On a fail, the receiver fetches _dmarc.corp.example and reads the policy.
p=none: deliver as usual but count it in the aggregate report. This is monitoring mode, the safe first step.
p=quarantine sends failing mail to spam; p=reject refuses it during the SMTP session, so it never reaches the mailbox.

Either way, the receiver can send daily (or more frequent) XML (Extensible Markup Language, a tagged text format) aggregate reports to the rua= address: which IPs sent as your domain, and how they fared.

blocks.md:
Two caveats from the standard. First, the policy is a request: RFC 9989 says receivers "can choose to honor" it "but it is not required", and DMARC is usually one input to filtering. The UK NCSC tells receivers to do as requested for quarantine and reject. Second, a pass "does not guarantee" that delivery would be "safe or desirable"; it says only that the domain's use was authorised.

**Rollout path.** Start with `p=none` and `rua=`; read the aggregate reports to find every legitimate service sending as you; fix their SPF and DKIM alignment; then move to `quarantine` and `reject` (optionally using `t=y` for a test period). [Gmail has required](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126) SPF, DKIM and a DMARC record (even at `p=none`) from senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts since February 2024.

blocks.code:
<record>
  <row>
    <source_ip>192.0.2.123</source_ip>
    <count>123</count>
    <policy_evaluated>
      <disposition>pass</disposition>
      <dkim>pass</dkim>
      <spf>fail</spf>
    </policy_evaluated>
  </row>
  <identifiers>
    <envelope_from>example.com</envelope_from>
    <header_from>example.com</header_from>
  </identifiers>
</record>
blocks.caption: One record of an aggregate report, from RFC 9990's example: 123 messages from 192.0.2.123 that failed SPF but passed DMARC through aligned DKIM. A source IP you do not recognise sending as your domain is either a forgotten vendor or a spoofer.

blocks.md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

blocks.question: corp.example publishes p=reject. A message arrives with From: billing@corp.example, SPF pass for mailer.example (not aligned), and a DKIM signature from corp.example that fails because a gateway edited the body. What is the DMARC result?
options: Fail, because no passing mechanism is aligned
Pass, because SPF passed
Pass, because the DKIM domain aligns
None, because the signature was edited
blocks.explain: DMARC needs a pass that is also aligned. SPF passed but for an unaligned domain; DKIM is aligned but failed. Neither qualifies, so DMARC fails and p=reject applies. Edits in transit are a known source of legitimate DMARC failures.

blocks.question: An attacker sends from payroll.corp.example, a subdomain that does not exist in DNS. corp.example's record is 'v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=none'. Without an np= tag, which policy applies?
options: reject, from p=
quarantine by default
No policy; non-existent domains are skipped
none, from sp=
blocks.explain: RFC 9989: if np= is absent, the sp= policy (if present) applies to non-existent subdomains, otherwise p=. Here that is none, so the spoof is delivered. Adding np=reject closes this gap, as gov.uk does.

lessons.title: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message

blocks.md:
An employee reports: "Dana (our CEO) wants an urgent wire, it feels odd." As an analyst you open the **raw headers** (in most mail apps: "show original" or "view message source"). Everything you learned so far is there, if you know which lines to believe.

Receiving servers write their verdicts in one header, **Authentication-Results** (RFC 8601). It starts with the **authserv-id**, the name of the server that did the checks, then one `method=result` entry per check, with properties saying what was checked: `smtp.mailfrom` for SPF's envelope domain, `header.d` for DKIM's signing domain, `header.from` for DMARC's Author Domain.

blocks.code:
Authentication-Results: mx.corp.example;
 spf=fail smtp.mailfrom=corp.example;
 dkim=none;
 dmarc=fail (p=none) header.from=corp.example
Received: from mail.cheap-host.example (mail.cheap-host.example [203.0.113.9])
 by mx.corp.example with ESMTPS; Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:14:02 +0000
Authentication-Results: mx.corp.example; spf=pass; dkim=pass; dmarc=pass
Received: from laptop (unknown [198.51.100.77])
 by mail.cheap-host.example with ESMTPSA; Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:13:58 +0000
From: "Dana Ruiz, CEO" <dana.ruiz@corp.example>
Reply-To: dana.ruiz.ceo@freemail.example
To: ap-team@corp.example
Subject: Urgent wire before 11:00
Date: Tue, 10 Mar 2026 09:13:55 +0000
Message-ID: <a1b2c3@cheap-host.example>

Can you process a payment today? I am in meetings, email only.
blocks.caption: The reported message, raw. Two Authentication-Results headers both claim to come from mx.corp.example. Only one can be real.

blocks.md:
Work top down, using what lessons 4 to 8 taught:

1. **Which Authentication-Results is yours?** Your border server prepends its header above its own Received line. The top one says `spf=fail`, `dkim=none`, `dmarc=fail`. The second one sits **below** your server's Received line, so it was already in the message when it arrived: the sender wrote it.
2. **Who connected?** Your server's Received line (the top one) saw `203.0.113.9`, calling itself `mail.cheap-host.example`. The lower Received line, naming a laptop at 198.51.100.77, was also written before your server got the message, so it is a claim.
3. **Do the identities agree?** From is `corp.example`, Reply-To is `freemail.example`, and the Message-ID was made at `cheap-host.example`.
4. **What does it ask for?** Urgency, secrecy, money: the BEC pattern of lesson 13.

RFC 8601 says a border server MUST delete any Authentication-Results header that claims its own authserv-id but did not come from a trusted server, and that mail apps should ignore these headers unless the hostname is on an explicit trusted list. Trust exactly one: the topmost from your own authserv-id.

blocks.prompt: A junior analyst's script searches the whole message for the text 'dmarc=pass' and marks a message safe if found. What does it say about this message?
blocks.reveal: It says **safe**. The attacker added `Authentication-Results: mx.corp.example; spf=pass; dkim=pass; dmarc=pass` lower in the headers, so the text is present. A compliant border server would have deleted it, but scripts must not rely on that. Parse only the topmost Authentication-Results carrying your own authserv-id, as the script below does.

blocks.title: A header triage script, run on the reported message

scenes.caption: Parse the raw text with Python's standard email library. policy.default gives structured access to address headers.
get_all returns Authentication-Results headers top first. The first one whose authserv-id is ours is the real verdict; the loop returns before reaching the forged one.
Every check that is not 'pass' becomes a flag.
Reply-To points to a different domain than From: a classic sign that replies are being diverted.
The connecting IP comes from the top Received header, written by our own MX. Lower Received lines are claims made before the message reached us.
The verdict. The script does not decide alone: it gives the analyst facts that are hard to fake.
scenes.output:
From:    Dana Ruiz, CEO <dana.ruiz@corp.example>
Sent by: 203.0.113.9 | hops: 2
Verdict: SUSPICIOUS ['spf=fail', 'dkim=none', 'dmarc=fail', 'reply-to domain freemail.example']

blocks.md:
Run it as `python3 triage.py suspect.eml`. The output above is the real output on the message shown. Why did this spoof reach an inbox at all? Look at the top header: `dmarc=fail (p=none)`. corp.example is still in DMARC monitoring mode, so its record expressed no preference and the receiver delivered the failure as normal. This is the cost of stopping at p=none.

**Defender view.** Prevention: move your domain to p=reject; tag external mail; flag display names that match executives on external addresses. Detection: alert on inbound mail where header From is your own domain and DMARC fails (nobody legitimate should do that once your senders are fixed). Response: search all mailboxes for the same sending IP, Message-ID domain and Reply-To address to find other recipients, then purge them (lesson 14).
Do not open links or attachments from a reported message on your own workstation while triaging. Read headers as text, and send URLs and files to a sandbox (lesson 11).

blocks.question: A message has two Authentication-Results headers: the top from mx.corp.example (dmarc=fail) and a lower one from mx.corp.example (dmarc=pass). Which do you trust?
options: The lower one, because it is older and closer to the sender
The top one, because it was added by your border server on arrival
Neither; Authentication-Results are always forged
Both; take the more favourable
blocks.explain: Your border server prepends its result on arrival, so the top one carrying your own authserv-id is yours. Anything lower was written before your server got the message. RFC 8601 says such forged copies should be deleted by the border server.

blocks.question: Which header detail is the hardest for an external sender to fake?
options: The display name in From
The IP address in the Received header written by your own border server
The bottom Received header's IP address
The Message-ID
blocks.explain: Your own server wrote that line using the address of the TCP connection it actually accepted. All the other fields, including lower Received lines, are text the sender (or a relay) controlled. Behind proxies or relays, it is the last hop rather than the true origin, but it is a fact, not a claim.

blocks.md:
Once a company publishes DMARC at p=reject, forging its exact domain stops working. So attackers register a domain that **looks like** it. They own that domain, so they can publish valid SPF, DKIM and DMARC for it, and every check passes.

Common shapes, using `corp.example` as the target:

- **Typo or character swap**: `c0rp.example`, `corp.exarnple` ("rn" reads as "m"). Brian Krebs, an investigative security journalist, describes BEC crews registering domains "one or two letters off", such as `examp1e.com` with the digit 1 for the letter l.
- **Added words**: `corp-example-billing.com`, `corpexample-support.com`.
- **Different top-level domain**: `corp.example.co`, or the same name under another suffix.
- **Subdomain tricks**: `corp.example.login-verify.net`, where the registered domain is really `login-verify.net`. Read domains right to left.

The hardest kind uses **homoglyphs**: characters from other alphabets that are drawn the same as Latin letters. Unicode, the standard that assigns a number (code point, written U+ and hex) to every character of every script, calls these **confusables** and publishes lists of them in Unicode Technical Standard 39 (UTS 39, "Unicode Security Mechanisms").

Domain names can contain non-Latin letters through **IDN** (internationalized domain names). Because host names in DNS are limited to ASCII letters, digits and hyphens (ASCII is the basic 128-character Latin set), each such label is converted to ASCII with **Punycode** (RFC 3492, "a simple and efficient transfer encoding syntax" for IDNA, Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications) and given the prefix `xn--`. So a domain that displays as "apple" can be a completely different name in DNS.

blocks.title: Two words that look identical

scenes.caption: Top: the Latin word 'apple'. Bottom: five Cyrillic letters. In most fonts the two rows render the same.
Their code points differ in every position. To DNS these are unrelated names: apple.com versus xn--80ak6aa92e.com.
The 'l' is U+04CF, Cyrillic small letter palochka, and the 'e' is U+0435, Cyrillic small letter ie. UTS 39 lists them as confusable with l and e.

blocks.code:
import unicodedata

def check(domain):
    label = domain.split(".")[0]
    ace = domain.encode("idna").decode()
    scripts = {unicodedata.name(ch).split()[0] for ch in label}
    flag = "MIXED" if len(scripts) > 1 else ""
    print(f"{ace:20} {sorted(scripts)} {flag}")

check("apple.com")
check("аpple.com")                     # Cyrillic a + Latin pple
check("аррӏе.com")   # every letter Cyrillic

# Output:
# apple.com            ['LATIN'] 
# xn--pple-43d.com     ['CYRILLIC', 'LATIN'] MIXED
# xn--80ak6aa92e.com   ['CYRILLIC']
blocks.caption: Python 3 standard library. The idna codec produces the xn-- form; unicodedata names each letter's script. Note the last line: all-Cyrillic passes a mixed-script check.

blocks.md: The script shows why one simple rule is not enough. A **mixed-script** check (flag labels that combine Latin and Cyrillic letters) catches `xn--pple-43d` but not the all-Cyrillic `xn--80ak6aa92e`, which UTS 39 calls a **whole-script confusable**. UTS 39's stronger tool is the **skeleton**: map every character to a representative look-alike, then two strings are confusable exactly when their skeletons are equal. Compute the skeleton of every domain in incoming mail and links and compare it with the skeletons of your own and your partners' domains.

**Case: Ubiquiti, 2015.** Ubiquiti Networks, a network-equipment maker, disclosed to the US SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) that it lost USD 46.7 million through employee impersonation and fraudulent requests from an outside entity targeting its finance department; it recovered USD 8.1 million. The company did not say exactly how it was fooled. Krebs's report on it explains the usual method: the attacker phishes an executive's mailbox, or emails staff from a lookalike domain, with Reply-To on the attacker's domain so every answer goes to them.

**Defender view.** Prevention: register the obvious variants of your own domain; keep a list of partner domains and flag mail from close relatives of them. Detection: skeleton and edit-distance matching (counting the single-character edits between two names) on sender domains and links; alerts on mail from domains registered in the last few days. Response: block the domain at the mail gateway and web proxy, search for other recipients, report it to the registrar.

Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

blocks.question: Which domain is actually controlled by whoever registered 'login-verify.net'?
options: login-verify.corp.example
corp.example
corp.example.login-verify.net
verify.corp.example
blocks.explain: Read right to left: corp.example.login-verify.net is a subdomain of login-verify.net, so its owner controls it. The other three are under corp.example.

blocks.question: A filter flags only domains that mix Latin and Cyrillic letters in one label. Which lookalike of 'apple.com' slips through?
options: xn--80ak6aa92e.com (all five letters Cyrillic)
xn--pple-43d.com (Cyrillic a + Latin pple)
apple.com
None; mixed-script checks catch every homoglyph
blocks.explain: All-Cyrillic labels are single-script, so a mixed-script rule passes them. UTS 39 calls this a whole-script confusable; skeleton comparison catches it.

lessons.title: Malicious links, attachments and HTML smuggling

blocks.md: A lure has to make the person do something. Almost always it is one of two things: **follow a link** or **open a file**. Start with links. In HTML email, what you see and where it goes are separate: the visible text of `Y` is Y, the destination is X. Y can even look like a URL. A **credential-harvest page** (a copy of a real login page whose form sends what you type to the attacker) sits at X. Its domain is a lookalike (lesson 10), a hacked legitimate site, or hidden behind a **URL shortener** (a service that turns a long address into a short one that redirects), as in the Podesta email of lesson 5.

blocks.code:
from html.parser import HTMLParser from urllib.parse import urlsplit class Links(HTMLParser): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.href, self.found = None, [] def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs): if tag == "a": self.href = dict(attrs).get("href", "") def handle_data(self, text): if self.href is not None: self.found.append((text.strip(), self.href)) self.href = None html = ('

Review the invoice at ' '' 'https://portal.corp.example/invoices

') p = Links() p.feed(html) for text, href in p.found: shown = urlsplit(text).hostname if "://" in text else None real = urlsplit(href).hostname print("shown:", shown, "| real:", real, "| MISMATCH" if shown and shown != real else "") # Output: # shown: portal.corp.example | real: login.corp-example.test | MISMATCH
blocks.caption: Python standard library: find links whose visible text names one host while the href goes to another. Real filters also follow redirects and expand shorteners.

blocks.md:
Now files. **Macros** are small programs embedded in Office documents, written in **VBA** (Visual Basic for Applications, the scripting language built into Microsoft Office). An "enable content" click lets a document's macro run with the user's rights, which made macro documents a staple of malware delivery. Microsoft's documentation calls VBA macros "a common way for malicious actors to gain access to deploy malware and ransomware", and Office now blocks macros by default in files from the internet.

How does Office know a file came from the internet? Windows attaches the **Mark of the Web** (MOTW), a marker recording that a file came from an untrusted location such as a browser download or an email attachment. Microsoft notes that MOTW only applies to files saved on NTFS (the standard Windows disk file system), which is one reason defenders also block attachment types they do not need, such as disk images, at the gateway.

**Case: RSA, March 2011.** Uri Rivner of RSA, the security company that made SecurID login tokens, described the intrusion in a blog post, "Anatomy of an Attack". Two phishing emails were sent over two days to two small groups of employees who were not especially high-profile. The subject was "2011 Recruitment Plan". One employee retrieved the message **from the Junk folder** and opened the attached spreadsheet, "2011 Recruitment plan.xls". It contained a **zero-day** (a flaw attackers exploit before the vendor has released a fix) in Adobe Flash, CVE-2011-0609 (a CVE, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, number is the public catalogue ID for one known flaw), which installed a variant of the Poison Ivy **RAT** (remote administration tool, Rivner's term; also called a remote access tool: software that lets an attacker control the machine), connecting outward to its controller. [Wired's 2021 account](https://www.wired.com/story/the-full-story-of-the-stunning-rsa-hack-can-finally-be-told/) reports that the intruders' final target was the secret "seed" values behind SecurID tokens.

blocks.title: RSA 2011: from a spreadsheet to stolen seeds

scenes.caption: A targeted email with a plausible HR subject reaches a few staff. The filter did its job: the message landed in Junk.
An employee pulls it out of Junk and opens the spreadsheet. The embedded Flash object exploits CVE-2011-0609.
A Poison Ivy backdoor is installed. It calls out to the attacker's server, which is harder to spot than an inbound connection.
The attackers move to more privileged accounts and servers, stage data internally, and send password-protected archives out over FTP, per Rivner.
Wired's 2021 account: the target was the 'seed' values behind SecurID tokens. Defender cuts: block legacy active content, keep Junk quarantined, alert on new outbound beacons.

blocks.md:
**HTML smuggling** is a newer delivery trick, listed by MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge: a public catalogue of attacker techniques run by the non-profit MITRE Corporation, whose name is not an acronym) as technique T1027.006. Concept only: the email carries an HTML file or links to a page whose JavaScript **builds the malicious file inside the browser** from data embedded in the page, using a Blob (a JavaScript object holding raw bytes) or a data URL (a link that carries the file's bytes inside the address itself), and then triggers a download. The mail gateway and web proxy see only ordinary text/html, so content filters looking for a dangerous file never see one.

Because the file is assembled on the endpoint, defence shifts there: block or neutralise HTML attachments from outside, rely on browser and endpoint scanning of the downloaded file (which still carries MOTW), and watch for archives or scripts created by the browser right after a user opened an HTML attachment.

Defender view for links and files: **URL rewriting** (the gateway replaces each link with one through its own scanner, so it can block a site that turns malicious after delivery), **sandboxing** (opening attachments and links in an isolated virtual machine and watching what they do before release), blocking macro-enabled and container file types from outside, and endpoint alerts when an Office app or browser spawns a script interpreter.

blocks.question: Why did RSA's spam filter not prevent the 2011 compromise?
options: The filter was disabled
The email came from an internal address
The email did land in Junk, but an employee retrieved it and opened the attachment
Flash files cannot be scanned
blocks.explain: Rivner wrote that the email was crafted well enough to trick an employee into retrieving it from Junk. A filter that moves mail to a folder users can browse is a soft control; quarantines users cannot release on their own are stronger.

blocks.question: A gateway inspects every attachment's file type and blocks executables. Why does HTML smuggling get past it?
options: The executable is created by JavaScript in the recipient's browser, so it never crosses the gateway as a file
The gateway cannot read HTML
HTML attachments are encrypted by SMTP
Executables inside HTML are always signed
blocks.explain: The gateway sees only an HTML document. The payload exists as encoded data and becomes a file only on the endpoint, which is why endpoint and browser controls matter here.

lessons.title: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and why passkeys resist it

blocks.md:
Many companies answered credential phishing with MFA: a password plus a six-digit code or a phone prompt. Attackers answered with **adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing**: instead of a static fake page, they run a **reverse proxy**, a server that sits between the victim and the real site and passes every request and response through.

One background idea first. After you log in, a website gives your browser a **session cookie**: a small random value the browser sends with every later request so the site knows it is still you. Whoever holds that cookie is logged in, without needing the password or MFA again. MITRE ATT&CK lists stealing it as technique [T1539](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/) and notes that open-source frameworks such as Evilginx2 and Muraena gather session cookies through a malicious proxy in phishing campaigns.

blocks.title: An AiTM proxy relays a full login, MFA included

scenes.caption: The victim follows a phishing link to the proxy's lookalike domain. The proxy fetches the real login page and shows it, so everything looks genuine.
The victim types their password. The proxy forwards it to the real site.
The real site asks for the MFA code; the proxy relays the question, and the victim's answer, both ways.
Login succeeds. The real site issues a session cookie; the proxy keeps a copy and can now use the account from anywhere, with no further MFA.

blocks.md:
Codes and push prompts fail here for the same reason they failed at Twitter (lesson 3): they are **not bound to the site**. A six-digit code works on whichever page the human types it into, and a "Approve sign-in?" prompt cannot know which page the person is looking at. The human is the relay.

**Passkeys** fix exactly that. A passkey is a **WebAuthn** credential (Web Authentication, the W3C browser standard; W3C is the World Wide Web Consortium, the web's standards body): a public/private key pair created for one site. The site stores the public key; the private key stays in the device (or in a password manager that syncs it, end-to-end encrypted, between your own devices) and is never sent to the site. CISA calls FIDO (Fast IDentity Online)/WebAuthn "the only widely available phishing-resistant authentication"; the FIDO Alliance is the industry group that created the protocol.

Three bindings in the WebAuthn standard defeat the proxy:

1. Each credential belongs to an **RP ID** (relying party ID: the site's domain, such as `corp.example`). The browser only allows a page to use an RP ID that is its own domain or a registrable parent of it, so a page on `login.corp-example.test` cannot ask for a `corp.example` credential at all (the only exception is an origin that corp.example itself publishes as related, which the attacker cannot do).
2. The browser, not the page, writes the real **origin** (scheme plus host) into `clientDataJSON`, and the authenticator signs a hash of it together with a hash of the RP ID. A proxy cannot edit either without breaking the signature.
3. The server must check that origin and RP ID hash before accepting, as below.

blocks.title: Server-side check: the proxy's origin gives it away

scenes.caption: The server knows its own RP ID and origin. These are fixed, not taken from the request.
Decode the clientDataJSON the browser produced. Its fields were filled in by the browser and are covered by the signature.
Type and challenge match: the challenge is a fresh random value from this login attempt, which stops replay of old responses.
The origin is the proxy's domain, not ours. The server rejects. (In practice the browser would already have refused to use a corp.example passkey there.)
When the user is really on login.corp.example, origin and RP ID hash match, and the server goes on to verify the signature with the stored public key.
scenes.output:
reject: origin https://login.corp-example.test
ok so far: now verify the signature with the stored public key

blocks.md:
Run with `node verify.mjs` (Node.js 18 or later). It is a sketch of the checks the WebAuthn spec lists for verifying an assertion (type is `webauthn.get`, challenge matches, origin is expected, RP ID hash matches, then the signature); use a maintained WebAuthn library in production rather than writing this yourself.

**What passkeys do not fix.** Payment fraud needs no login at all (lesson 13). Malware already on the laptop can steal a session cookie after a legitimate login. And account **recovery** becomes the weak point: if the help desk will reset a passkey account to a password on a phone call, the MGM-style attack of lesson 3 still works. NYDFS concluded hardware security keys would have stopped the Twitter attackers; that holds only if recovery is equally strict.

Defender view: detect AiTM by its traces. A session cookie used from a new IP address or country minutes after sign-in, sign-ins from hosting providers, and new inbox rules that hide or forward mail (MITRE T1564.008, a frequent next step toward BEC). Respond by revoking all sessions and refresh tokens (long-lived tokens an app uses to get new sessions without a new login), not only resetting the password: the stolen cookie, not the password, is the attacker's access.

blocks.question: A user on an AiTM phishing page enters their password and a correct six-digit TOTP code (time-based one-time password, the code an authenticator app shows). What does the attacker end up with?
options: Nothing, because the code expires in 30 seconds
Only the password, because MFA stops the login
The user's private key
A valid session cookie for the real site, obtained by relaying the code in time
blocks.explain: The proxy forwards the code immediately, while it is still valid. The real site completes the login and issues a session cookie, which the proxy keeps.

blocks.question: Why can't an AiTM proxy simply forward a passkey login the same way?
options: Passkeys are too long to forward
The browser binds the credential to the site's domain and signs the real origin, so the proxy's domain gets no usable credential or a signature the server rejects
Passkeys only work offline
The proxy cannot read HTTPS traffic
blocks.explain: The proxy terminates HTTPS itself, so it can read traffic. What it cannot do is make the browser use a corp.example credential on its own domain, or change the signed origin. That is origin binding.

blocks.question: After an AiTM incident, the help desk resets the victim's password. Why is that not enough?
options: Passwords cannot be reset remotely
The attacker's stolen session cookie may stay valid until sessions are revoked
The attacker also needs the new password to keep reading mail
Password resets delete the mailbox
blocks.explain: The attacker never needed the password after login; the cookie is the access. Revoke sessions and tokens, remove attacker-added MFA methods and inbox rules, then reset.

lessons.title: Business email compromise and invoice fraud

blocks.md:
Some of the costliest phishing never steals a password or installs anything. It just asks for money in the right voice at the right moment.

The FBI's IC3 defines **business email compromise** (BEC) as a scam that targets businesses and individuals who perform legitimate transfer-of-funds requests, often carried out by compromising real business or personal email accounts through social engineering or computer intrusion to make unauthorised transfers. Its 2024 public service announcement counted 305,033 domestic and international incidents with USD 55.5 billion in exposed losses between October 2013 and December 2023; the 2025 annual report alone lists USD 3.05 billion.

The main variants:

- **CEO fraud**: a message as an executive to someone who can pay ("urgent wire, keep it quiet"). Uses display-name spoofs, lookalike domains, or exact-domain spoofs where DMARC is not enforced.
- **Vendor or invoice fraud**: the attacker poses as a supplier and sends a bill or a "new bank details" letter. The amounts look normal because they are copies of normal ones.
- **Account compromise**: the attacker has logged into a real mailbox (often by AiTM phishing, lesson 12), reads ongoing threads, and replies inside them at the moment an invoice is due. Every authentication check passes, because it is the real account.

**Case: Evaldas Rimasauskas, 2013 to 2015.** Rimasauskas, a Lithuanian national, posed as Quanta, a Taiwanese manufacturer that really did build servers and other hardware for Facebook and Google. CyberScoop reports that they created domains spoofing Quanta and sent fraudulent invoices directing the companies' employees to wire money, netting about USD 99 million from Facebook and USD 23 million from Google.
